the_line: Lean proves that a conclusion follows from stated premises. It does not adjudicate reality. Every theorem in this repo is of the form 'if these premises hold, then this follows', and a kernel proof of it is silent on whether any organism satisfies the premises. So a grand question has a formalisable core exactly to the extent that part of the disagreement about it is a disagreement about what follows from what, and an empirical remainder exactly to the extent that it is a disagreement about what the world is like. Most of these questions are mostly remainder. Two of them (the Price equation, Hamilton's rule) are disputes in which the formal part has been repeatedly confused with the empirical part for decades, and those are the ones where formalisation would do the most good. A capability map that let the first kind of progress be read as the second would be worse than no map.
name: The major evolutionary transitions
question: Why did replicators become chromosomes, cells become eukaryotes, individuals become societies? What makes a transition in individuality happen, and why so rarely?

statements.claim: If an asexual variant has a twofold reproductive advantage factor and starts at frequency q, then its frequency after n generations is determined, so a claim that sex persists without a compensating benefit of at least that size does not follow.
statements.settles: The arithmetic of the cost of sex, which is the quantitative core of the sex transition. It settles the size of the benefit that any explanation must supply; it does not identify the benefit.

statements.claim: If a transition requires a stated number of substitutions and the population and mutation parameters are stated, then the available time bounds whether it could occur at all.
statements.settles: Whether a proposed transition route is reachable, as a budget question. Our Haldane-cost law does exactly this FROM a named hypothesis, and the registry records that the hypothesis itself has been contested since 1957.

statements.claim: If a multilevel population has stated within- and between-group fitnesses and a stated group structure, then the direction of change in the group-level character follows from the Price partition, so a claimed direction inconsistent with the partition is impossible.
statements.settles: Whether a verbal argument about a transition's direction is an algebraic consequence of its own stated structure. Requires the Price equation, which this repo does not have.

items.what: Which selective force actually drove each transition.
items.why_not_provable: A historical cause, and in several cases the evidence is a single lineage.
items.measurement: Comparative phylogenetics plus experimental evolution of de novo transitions; for the deepest transitions, no measurement exists.

items.what: Whether each transition happened once or repeatedly, and what the ancestral states were.
items.measurement: Phylogenomics; palaeontology where there is a record.

items.what: Whether sex is maintained by recombination's effect on deleterious mutation load, by host-parasite dynamics, or by something else.
items.why_not_provable: Every candidate benefit is formally capable of exceeding the twofold cost. Which one does is empirical.
items.measurement: Experimental evolution with recombination rate manipulated and load measured directly.

in_repo.note: The twofold cost proved both for one generation and iterated over n, with the frequency staying in the unit interval proved separately.
The second is explicitly a theorem FROM a named hypothesis, and its registry note says the hypothesis has been contested since 1957. That labelling is the point.

in_repo.note: The origin and the maintenance of sex are enumerated separately with sourced statements, and a formal candidate exists for WP-002.

Two frequency-dependent-selection results proved from named hypotheses (Shaw-Mohler fitness; the Hawk-Dove payoff matrix). They bear on sex allocation and on mixed strategies, not on the transitions themselves, so they are adjacent: the idiom and the machinery are here, pointed at a neighbouring question.

scope: This is a map of what is formalisable, not a research programme and not a claim that the formalisable parts are the important parts. The (a)/(b) split is a judgement made here and is arguable for every entry; where it is contentious the dispute field says so. The list is not exhaust: there is no canonical set of grand questions in biology, and this one is weighted toward evolution, development and scaling because that is what this project reads. Several entries have no counterpart in open-problems/problems.json, which is a gap in that enumeration rather than evidence the question is settled. Nothing here is about the held-out exam clade.
